title: A toll at Aydhab
body: Hamza leads caravans to the Red Sea. A caravan is a group of travellers and animals that go together. At Aydhab a toll, a fee to pass, is taken on every load. Hamza asks every house that sends goods his way to pay a share.

choices.label: Pay a share of the toll
choices.hint: It costs now. Hamza will speak well of you.

choices.label: Send goods by Quseir instead
choices.hint: It costs less, later. Quseir is nearer to Qus, and partners like a house that counts its costs.

note: Ibn Battuta saw Aydhab in 1326. One third of the town was the sultan's, and two thirds was the Beja king's. A writer of about 1400 says some merchants preferred Quseir, because it was nearer Qus.

sources.at: pp. 33 and 35; Quseir nearer Qus, and the split of Aydhab's revenue (sometimes in half)
vol. 1, p. 68; one third of the city the sultan's, two thirds the Beja king's, in 1326

title: The officer counts twice
body: Your carters wait at Alexandria to bring a merchant's goods up from a ship. A customs officer there has not met your house, so he counts every bundle twice. Customs are taxes on goods that enter a port. He asks for 5 dinars.

choices.label: Pay it all and ask for a receipt
choices.hint: It costs now. Your name goes in his book.

choices.label: Leave the goods in the harbour store
choices.hint: It costs less. Your goods wait and the officer notices, but partners like a patient house.

note: A merchant's handbook from about 1340 says goods coming into Alexandria paid 20 in every hundred. Goods going out paid nothing.

sources.at: print p. 72; the duty at Alexandria

title: A stranger needs a name
body: Giorgio is new in Alexandria. The port officers do not know him, but they know your house. He asks you to vouch for him, to tell them he will pay what he owes. If he does not pay, they will come to you.

choices.label: Vouch for Giorgio
choices.hint: He will not forget it. His debt could become yours.

choices.label: Say you do not know him
choices.hint: You keep your money. The port officers like a house that knows whom it vouches for.

note: Merchants had long done favours for each other and expected the same. One Geniza letter says: "you are in my place there, for you know well that I am your support here."

sources.at: p. 316; business friends who serve each other

title: Papers for the road
body: Nabil belongs to the Karimi, a loose group of merchants who trade spices. One writer says a spice office gave them papers for the road. It took 2.5 in every hundred of their goods. He says he could carry two loads for your house under his papers.

choices.label: Send two loads under his papers
choices.hint: It costs 5 dinars for the papers. Nabil will be glad to help.

choices.label: Go without his papers
choices.hint: It costs less. Nabil may feel left out, but the officers see your own count.

note: One modern writer says the Karimi office gave its members papers. He says it took 2.5 in every hundred of their goods. The Karimi were a loose group, and historians do not agree on how tightly they were organised.

sources.at: pp. 150 and 152; a loose confederation; the office's papers and 2.5 percent are al-Ashqar's reading, as Sato reports it, and Sato takes the office for a state one
